Appendix C specifies the parameter models, reference values, and sampler updates. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental protocol We evaluate UAL at two levels: reconstruction and ensemble prediction in paired sampler comparisons (Section 4.2 ), and, at shared candidate images, likelihood and image-score accuracy against numerical nuisance marginalization (Section 4.3 ). Additional controls examine covariance structure, recomputation and differentiation, uncertainty level, and retained rank. Published denotes the released sampler and UAL its uncertainty-aware version; each pair uses the same measurement data, diffusion checkpoint, sampling schedule, step sizes, and reconstruction seeds.

Deblurring, CT, MRI, and microscopy use 50 cases, and ultrasound uses the acquired PICMUS contrast and resolution phantoms provided with DRUS; each case has 12 reconstruction seeds. The fixed deblurring ablation set contains 16 images, with 12 paired reconstruction seeds per image. Appendix C gives forward models, nuisance models, and sampler updates. We report PSNR and SSIM both as the mean over trajectories and for the ensemble-mean reconstruction. CRPS, energy, and local variogram scores (lower is better) use the fair finite-ensemble estimators of Appendix C.7 , which also gives the scoring coordinates and interval construction; ultrasound uses native contrast and resolution metrics. 4.2 Reconstruction across samplers and applications We compare the Published and UAL versions of DAPS, PnP-DM, DiffPIR, and BlindDPS for Gaussian and motion deblurring on FFHQ images ( Karras et al., 2019 ) (Table 1 ). The Gaussian setting uses kernel widths with mean s ¯ = 3 \bar{s}=3 pixels and standard deviation τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 pixels. In motion deblurring, each non-blind pair uses the population-mean kernel, giving the two likelihoods the same mean response at a common candidate image. Motion deblurring also includes Fast Diffusion EM ( Laroche et al., 2024 ) , a blind sampler that estimates a kernel for each image. Its UAL image update uses the population-mean kernel instead, with covariance accounting for image and kernel uncertainty and their interaction. We estimate the kernel covariance and retain its leading 256 eigenmodes ( P = 256 P=256 ), with this rank fixed before the covariance-rank sweep (Section 4.3 ). In motion deblurring, DAPS and PnP-DM with UAL exceed the published blind samplers BlindDPS and Fast Diffusion EM, which sample or estimate a kernel for each image, by 6.2 to 6.4 dB in ensemble-mean PSNR, with paired 95% intervals excluding zero (Table 9 ). For mean per-trajectory PSNR, UAL gives 28.84 dB for DAPS and 26.54 dB for PnP-DM, compared with 30.65 and 27.65 dB when the published samplers use the true kernel (Table 8 ). UAL also improves reconstruction and ensemble prediction in CT, MRI, and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1 ). Mean per-trajectory PSNR increases on all 50 CT detector rows, 47 of 50 MRI scans, and 43 of 50 microscopy sections. For CT, the gain persists when both versions use the same mean flat and dark reference fields (Appendix D ). For MRI under the Gaussian coil-sensitivity model, UAL gives the exact marginal measurement likelihood. The MRI reconstruction gains are small but consistent: all seven reported metrics improve, with pointwise 95% paired-bootstrap intervals excluding zero. On the acquired PICMUS ultrasound contrast phantom, UAL increases CNR from 9.929 to 12.363 dB and gCNR from 0.9141 to 0.9743. 4.3 Likelihood validation and controls Likelihood approximation. We next test whether covariance structure improves reconstruction and ensemble prediction beyond increasing total variance, using the three likelihoods in deblurring with PnP-DM. UAL and the isotropic control both include Gaussian normalization and differentiate their signal-dependent covariance. UAL’s structured covariance increases per-trajectory PSNR and reduces CRPS relative to trace-matched isotropic inflation in both tasks (Table 2 ). We also test fixed noise-variance multipliers and, for each task, report the one with the highest mean per-trajectory PSNR on the same ablation set used for comparison.

The best tested values give 27.029 dB ( v = 3 v=3 ) in Gaussian and 23.369 dB ( v = 48 v=48 ) in motion deblurring, compared with 27.475 and 26.641 dB for UAL (Appendix D.4 ). For DAPS in motion deblurring, the best tested multiplier of its data-term variance ( v = 48 v=48 ) gives 24.413 dB mean per-trajectory PSNR, compared with 28.631 dB for UAL on the ablation set. At the final UAL reconstructions in Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, nuisance variation adds about 20% to the average whitened measurement variance, carried by the two width-sensitivity responses (Appendix D.5 ). In Gaussian deblurring with PnP-DM, two further controls separate recomputing the covariance from differentiating it (Table 3 ). Fixing the covariance at the published sampler’s ensemble mean removes nearly all of the PSNR gain and raises CRPS above the published sampler’s.
